To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the mercury emissions of the chlorine production plants are in the range of 2 to 10 kg per year and plant, and that 2) this emission is a result of the decomposition of mercury containing solid wastes.
The amount of Hg emitted from the solid waste deposits of chlorine-producing plants is negligible.
the total mercury emission from the chlorine-producing solid waste deposits is about 1.3 tons/year and the emission rate is 0.3 g/ton of chlorine produced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the environmental impact of the chlor- alkali industry in the UK.
the environmental impact of Hg from the chlorine-production industry.
the fate and environmental impact of Hg emissions from solid waste deposits at the site of a decommissioned chlorine-production facility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chlor-alkai industry, as a source of atmospheric Hg emissions, is not important on a global basis.
the contribution of the chlor- alkali industry to the global cycling of Hg has been overestimated, but that it has a significant effect in some regions.
, although the chlor-alkalis are the major industrial Hg sources, the contribution to total global Hg cycling is relatively small.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chlor-alkai industry is a significant contributor to the global mercury cycle.
the chlor-alkalis have a significant role in the Hg cycle.
the chlor-alkalis are the largest single industrial source of mercury in the world, and that the industry is the largest single source of mercury in many regions of the world.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are still large quantities of mercury in solid waste from chlorine production, and that these wastes are not well characterized.
the mercury emission rates from the solid waste deposits at chlor-alkali plants are not negligible.
Hg emissions from chlorine production solid waste deposits can be significant, and the Hg emissions from these deposits can be controlled by covering the deposits with impermeable material.
